core: The working definition of the accounting cycle: the repeating sequence of steps that turns a period's transactions into financial statements, attributed to OpenStax's Principles of Accounting
The seven steps named, each in one line: identify transactions, record journal entries, post to the ledger, prepare a trial balance, make adjusting entries, prepare statements, close the books
Why the cycle matters: order prevents chaos (the general argument)
The cycle vs the equation: the cycle is the process, the equation is the check
Periodicity: the cycle repeats monthly or yearly over the accounting period
Who runs it: bookkeepers and accountants, each named
The honest framing: the cycle is repetitive by design, and the repetition is what catches errors
supporting: The equation as the consistency check on recording: every transaction must leave both sides of the equation with an equal net effect (CFI Accounting Equation; OpenStax Section 3.2)
The bookkeeper's role in running the cycle from start to finish (CFI Accounting Cycle; CFI Bookkeeping)
Textbooks number the steps differently (OpenStax nine-step split; CFI eight steps with a worksheet), so the lesson uses a simplified seven-step list
outOfScope: Journal entries and how entries are structured (sibling topic: accounting:foundations:journal-entries; referenced only)
The general ledger and how accounts are organized (sibling topic: accounting:foundations:general-ledger; referenced only)
The trial balance and what it checks (sibling topic: accounting:foundations:trial-balance; referenced only)
Adjusting entries in detail (sibling topic: accounting:foundations:adjusting-entries; referenced only)
The income statement's structure and preparation (sibling topic: accounting:foundations:income-statement; referenced only)
The accounting equation's full mechanics (sibling topic: accounting:foundations:accounting-equation; referenced only)
Balance sheet and cash flow statement preparation (sibling topics: balance-sheet, statement-of-cash-flows; referenced only)

claims.claim: The accounting cycle is a step-by-step process to record business activities and events to keep financial records up to date; it runs over one accounting period and begins again in the following period.
An accounting period can be a month, a quarter, or a year, and the cycle repeats for as long as the company remains in business.

The cycle's steps in their common simplified order are: identify transactions, record journal entries, post to the ledger, prepare a trial balance, make adjusting entries, prepare the financial statements, and close the books.

Textbooks number the steps differently: OpenStax splits the trial balance and closing into nine steps, and CFI counts eight including a worksheet step, so the exact count is a convention rather than a rule.
The cycle keeps financial data organized and easily accessible to both internal and external users of information.
Keeping track of the full accounting cycle from start to finish is one of a bookkeeper's main duties.
The accounting equation must always balance, and every transaction must leave both sides of the equation with an equal net effect; the equation is the consistency check on the cycle's recording.
Adjusting entries are posted at the end of the accounting period for accruals and deferrals, and closing zeroes out revenue and expense accounts so the next period starts fresh.
The cycle is repetitive by design: running the same steps in the same order each period is what catches recording errors.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The number of steps in the accounting cycle differs across textbooks.
positions: OpenStax presents nine steps, splitting the trial balance into unadjusted and adjusted versions and adding a post-closing trial balance (Principles of Accounting, Section 3.3)
CFI presents eight steps, including a separate worksheet step (Accounting Cycle guide)
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses the common simplified list of seven steps and says plainly that textbooks count them differently; each step's detail belongs to a sibling lesson.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Who is primarily responsible for running the cycle.
positions: CFI emphasizes the bookkeeper: one of a bookkeeper's main duties is to keep track of the full cycle from start to finish
OpenStax frames the accountant as the professional who designs and checks the process, with forensic accountants retracing the cycle's records
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson names both: bookkeepers run the day-to-day recording steps, and accountants design, analyze, and check the system and prepare the statements.

rightsIssues.issue: OpenStax's footer states the book may not be used to train large language models or be ingested into generative AI offerings without permission.
rightsIssues.handling: Lesson text was written from research notes as original prose; the working definition is paraphrased with attribution and no source wording is reproduced; the registry classifies OpenStax usage as EXTRACT_AND_ADAPT with the restriction noted.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Accounting, Volume 1: Financial Accounting, Section 3.3: Define and Describe the Initial Steps in the Accounting Cycle
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (open textbook). Read live via HTTP on 2026-08-21 (openstax.org). Supports: the accounting cycle as a step-by-step process to record business activities and events to keep financial records up to date; the process occurring over one accounting period (a month, quarter, or year) and beginning again in the following period; the named steps (identify and analyze transactions, record to a journal, post to a ledger, prepare an unadjusted trial balance, record adjusting entries, prepare an adjusted trial balance, prepare financial statements, closing entries, post-closing trial balance); the cycle keeping financial data organized and easily accessible to both internal and external users; original source documents such as a sales invoice as the starting point of transaction analysis. Facts synthesized into original prose; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Accounting Cycle — 8 Steps in the Accounting Cycle, Diagram, Guide
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B reference. Read live via HTTP on 2026-08-21. Supports: the accounting cycle as the holistic process of recording and processing all financial transactions of a company, from when a transaction occurs to its representation on the financial statements to closing the accounts; one of a bookkeeper's main duties being to keep track of the full accounting cycle from start to finish; the cycle repeating every fiscal year as long as a company remains in business; the named steps (transactions, journal entries, posting to the general ledger, trial balance, worksheet, adjusting entries, financial statements, closing); adjusting entries posted at the end of the accounting period for accruals and deferrals; closing zeroing out revenue and expense accounts while balance sheet accounts are not closed. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Accounting, Volume 1: Financial Accounting, Section 3.2: Define and Describe the Expanded Accounting Equation and Its Relationship to Analyzing Transactions
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (open textbook). Verified directly from the live OpenStax page on 2026-08-21. Supports the conceptual content of the accounting equation: a company needs assets to operate, and the two sources are liabilities (borrowed funds) and equity (owners' funds and profits); also confirms that the equation governs how transactions are recorded.

sourceRecords.title: Accounting Equation
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B (reputable secondary). Verified directly on 2026-08-21. Supports: the equation assets = liabilities + shareholders' equity; the equation as the foundation of double-entry accounting; the balance-sheet structure the equation highlights; and the mechanism by which an increase in an asset is matched by an equal increase in a liability or equity account (or an equal decrease in another asset) so the equation stays in balance.

sourceRecords.title: What is Bookkeeping? Definition & Process Explained
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B (reputable secondary). Verified directly on 2026-08-21. Supports bookkeeping as the recording process — the routine daily capture of transactions — that supports accurate financial reporting, tax preparation, and business decision-making, and thus the lesson's bookkeeping-vs-accounting distinction (recording vs interpreting).
